where: Section 2, m-adjacency bullet, and Exam traps item 3
problem: The formal rule is written as 'q ∈ ND(p) and N4(p) ∩ N4(q) is empty'. The standard definition requires the intersection to contain no pixels whose values are in V, not to be literally empty. In a grey-level or multi-valued image the two side pixels can exist with values outside V, and then the diagonal m-link is still allowed; the rule as written wrongly rejects it.
fix: m-adjacency: q ∈ N4(p), or q ∈ ND(p) and the set N4(p) ∩ N4(q) contains no pixels whose values are in V. Exam trap: N4(p) ∩ N4(q) must have no pixels with values in V, not simply be empty.

where: Section 3, sentence before the worked example
problem: 'None of these distances decides adjacency' contradicts the worked example and the quiz, where D4 = 1 is used to test 4-adjacency and D8 = 1 to test 8-adjacency. A student will not know which statement to trust.
fix: Say: 'Euclidean distance never decides adjacency. On the grid, D4 = 1 exactly when q ∈ N4(p) and D8 = 1 exactly when q ∈ N8(p), so the grid distances do match N4 and N8; only De is irrelevant to adjacency.'

problem: Adjacency also requires both intensities to lie in V, but the example never states V or the pixel values, so 'they are 8-adjacent' is only a geometric statement, not the full definition given in Section 2.
fix: Add: 'Assume both pixels have values in the chosen set V (for a binary object image, V = {1}). D4 = 2 ≠ 1 so not 4-adjacent; D8 = 1 so they are 8-adjacent.'

where: Section 2, boundary sentence, and Quiz Q7
problem: 'At least one neighbour outside the region' does not say which neighbourhood. Most textbooks fix the 4-neighbourhood for the boundary, so the loose wording leaves the definition ambiguous.
fix: A boundary pixel of a region R is a pixel of R that has at least one 4-neighbour not in R (state the neighbourhood explicitly; an 8-neighbour version is used only when the text says so).
